faqs.question: What is the SENTERRA II Raman Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: The SENTERRA II is a confocal Raman microscope used for failure analysis, quality control, and scientific research, across pharmaceuticals, forensics, polymers, and environmental testing.

faqs.question: What is SureCal, and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: SureCal is a patented technology that continuously recalibrates the SENTERRA II in the background, holding sub-wavenumber precision without a manual recalibration step interrupting analysis.

faqs.question: How many lasers does the SENTERRA II support?
faqs.answer: Bruker's own materials state one-click switching between 4 built-in lasers as a technical feature, and separately reference up to 3 excitation lasers for material science applications. Inkarp confirms the exact configuration for your application.

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II safe for students or first-time operators?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Class 1 laser housing with interlock protects the user from harmful laser radiation at all times, without requiring laser safety training.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II identify unknown substances automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, using A.I.D., an AI-driven tool that matches spectral data against reference databases in seconds, for pure substances or complex mixtures.

faqs.question: How do I identify an unknown chemical sample step by step with the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Select a built-in laser with one click, place the sample under the microscope, and start the measurement. A.I.D. then runs the identification automatically against reference spectral databases, returning a match with diagnostics and hit-quality graphs in seconds.

faqs.question: Can it generate a chemical image without selecting a Raman peak first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Adaptive K-means Clustering sorts spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own.

faqs.question: How do I generate a chemical image of a mixed or heterogeneous sample using the SENTERRA II?
faqs.answer: Run Adaptive K-means Clustering after the measurement, without selecting a specific Raman peak first. The software sorts the spectra into groups automatically and builds the chemical image on its own, showing at a glance whether the sample is homogeneous or structured.

faqs.question: Can the SENTERRA II be configured for live cell or tissue research?
faqs.answer: Yes, with the inverted microscope configuration, which gives open sample access without compromising functionality.

faqs.question: Is the SENTERRA II suitable for a regulated pharmaceutical environment?
faqs.answer: Yes. It's 100% compliant with GMP, major pharmacopoeias, and 21 CFR Part 11, and follows the ALCOA+ principle for data integrity.

faqs.question: Can Raman and infrared data be correlated from the same sample spot?
faqs.answer: Yes, using Co-Local Measurement, which transfers overview images and measurement areas between SENTERRA II, LUMOS II, and HYPERION II.

faqs.answer: The price depends on the configuration and software packages your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

sections.title: Continuous Calibration and Laser Safety
sections.tabSummary: How SureCal and Class 1 safety work together
body: Every Raman microscope drifts. Heat, component wear, and vibration all shift wavenumber accuracy over time, and most systems handle that with a scheduled recalibration routine that takes the instrument offline.

SureCal removes that step entirely, recalibrating continuously in the background so precision holds without a pause in analysis. That matters whether you're running a quick material identification or collecting a large dataset for PCA or other statistical work, where consistency across hundreds of measurements is the whole point. Laser safety runs on the same always-on principle: the Class 1 housing and interlock protect the user in every operating mode, which is what makes SENTERRA II usable by students and first-time operators without a separate safety program.

products.overview: A conventional Raman microscope scans a sample the way you'd read a page: top to bottom, left to right, no matter what you're actually looking for. RAMANwalk doesn't. It searches for the Raman signal itself, using a random-walk algorithm that follows chemical information rather than a fixed pattern. Find a signal, search around it, move on when it thins out. The result isn't just faster, it's faster at the question that matters. Looking for a contaminant in a sample where the full scan takes 50 minutes, RAMANwalk reaches a conclusive answer in about 5. In that same 5 minutes, a traditional raster scan is only 10% through the sample, with nothing found yet. Galvanic mirrors steer the beam instead of moving the stage, spatial resolution runs to 350 nm, and the whole system calibrates and aligns itself automatically.

faqs.question: What is the RAMANwalk Raman Microscope used for?
faqs.answer: The RAMANwalk is a confocal Raman microscope used for fast Raman imaging and targeted material identification, across battery research, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, and food quality control.

faqs.question: What is random-walk imaging?
faqs.answer: Random-walk imaging is a search algorithm that finds and follows the Raman signal directly, rather than scanning a sample in a fixed pattern regardless of what's present.

faqs.question: How much faster is RAMANwalk than a conventional Raman microscope?
faqs.answer: More than 5 times faster for obtaining Raman images, and on a targeted question like contamination detection, RAMANwalk can reach a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes where a conventional raster scan is only 10% complete in the same time.

faqs.question: How do I get a fast preview of an unknown sample with the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: Start the random-walk scan and watch the preview build: rough detail appears within seconds to a minute, finer detail within a few minutes, letting you decide whether the sample is worth a full-resolution scan before committing to the full run time.

faqs.question: How do I check a sample for a specific contaminant quickly with the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: Run the random-walk search targeted at the contaminant's Raman signature rather than a full scan. On a comparable real sample, this reached a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, versus roughly 50 minutes for a complete image.

faqs.question: Can RAMANwalk find signal in low-contrast samples?
faqs.answer: Yes. It locates regions of interest using chemical Raman information, even when the sample gives no useful visual contrast.

faqs.question: What is the spatial resolution of the RAMANwalk?
faqs.answer: 350 nm in X and Y, and 1 µm in Z.

faqs.question: How many objective lenses does the RAMANwalk offer?
faqs.answer: Five: 5x, 10x, 20x, 50x, and 100x, covering broad overview imaging through fine sub-micron detail.

faqs.question: Does the RAMANwalk need manual calibration?
faqs.answer: No. It auto-calibrates against a standard lamp and sample, and auto-aligns its own optical path.

faqs.question: Is the RAMANwalk safe to use without laser safety training?
faqs.answer: Yes. It has a Class I laser safety housing with an interlocked door, protecting the user at all times.

faqs.answer: The price depends on the objective and grating configuration your application needs. Contact Inkarp for a quotation once your requirements are confirmed.

sections.tabSummary: How the algorithm finds an answer faster than a scan
body: A conventional Raman microscope treats every point in a sample as equally worth visiting. RAMANwalk doesn't.

The random-walk algorithm finds a distinctive Raman signal, searches the surrounding area for more of it, and moves rapidly elsewhere once the signal runs out. It's a fundamentally different search strategy, not just a faster version of the old one, and it's why RAMANwalk delivers a rough preview in under a minute and finer detail within a few minutes, well before a full scan would even be close to done. On a real contamination question, that difference is the whole point: a conclusive answer in about 5 minutes, against a traditional raster scan that's only 10% complete in the same time, with nothing found yet.

longForm.heroHook: It doesn't scan everything. It walks straight to the answer.
heroParagraphs: A conventional Raman microscope scans a sample the way you'd read a page: top to bottom, left to right, no matter what you're actually looking for.

RAMANwalk doesn't. It searches for the Raman signal itself, using a random-walk algorithm that follows chemical information rather than a fixed pattern. Find a signal, search around it, move on when it thins out.

The result isn't just faster, it's faster at the question that matters. Looking for a contaminant in a sample where the full scan takes 50 minutes, RAMANwalk reaches a conclusive answer in about 5. In that same 5 minutes, a traditional raster scan is only 10% through the sample, with nothing found yet.
Galvanic mirrors steer the beam instead of moving the stage, spatial resolution runs to 350 nm, and the whole system calibrates and aligns itself automatically.
longForm.statsIntro: The quick stats of the RAMANwalk Raman Microscope cover its scan speed, resolution, and automation.
